title: Real Work v. Real World
author: Dan Meyer
summary: Dan Meyer republishes an older post that revised his early theory of student engagement in math. He once believed students engage when the math is set in the real world, but found the theory fails because students dislike some real-world problems and enjoy some purely mathematical ones. His fix adds a second axis: not only the realness of a problem's world but the realness of the work students do inside it, with real work meaning problem formulation and question development. Teachers are therefore wrong to expect that mobile-phone themes will fix boring tasks. He concludes that we overrate interest in fake work in the real world and underrate interest in real work in the fake world. The surrounding roundup of AI links is secondary to the throwback essay.
points: Real-world context alone does not explain engagement, because students can find real-world tasks boring and abstract ones fascinating.
Meyer adds a second axis, the work students do, separating fake calculation from real work such as formulating questions.
Making the problem about phones removes 'When will I ever use this?' but leaves the underlying questions boring.
The richest design space is real work in a fake world.
quotes: But the theory that “students are engaged in math if and only if the math is real world” fails. It fails to account for real world math problems that students dislike. And it fails to account for pure math problems that students enjoy.

But teachers report time and again that these tasks don’t measurably move the needle on student engagement in challenging mathematics. They’re real world, so students are disarmed of their usual question, “When will I ever use this?” But the questions are still boring.
That’s because there is a second axis we focus on less. That axis looks at work. It looks at what students do.
Real work — interesting work, the sort of work students might like to do later in life — involves problem formulation and question development.

We overrate student interest in doing fake work in the real world. We underrate student interest in doing real work in the fake world. There is so much gold in that top-left quadrant. There is much less gold than we think in the bottom-right.
